claim: Cephalopod mollusks evolved numerous anatomical novelties, including arms and tentacles.
source: Cephalopod mollusks evolved numerous anatomical novelties, including arms and tentacles, but little is known about the developmental mechanisms underlying cephalopod limb evolution.
evidence: This is a statement about cephalopod evolution presented in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: All three axes of cuttlefish limbs are patterned by the same signaling networks that act in vertebrates and arthropods.
source: Here we show that all three axes of cuttlefish limbs are patterned by the same signaling networks that act in vertebrates and arthropods, although they evolved limbs independently.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression and functional data presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Cephalopods, vertebrates, and arthropods evolved limbs independently.
source: Here we show that all three axes of cuttlefish limbs are patterned by the same signaling networks that act in vertebrates and arthropods, although they evolved limbs independently.
evidence: This is based on established phylogenetic knowledge and the absence of homologous structures across these lineages.

claim: Hedgehog is expressed anteriorly in cuttlefish limb buds.
source: In cuttlefish limb buds, Hedgehog is expressed anteriorly.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D, K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Posterior transplantation of Hedgehog-expressing cells induced mirror-image limb duplications in cuttlefish.
source: Posterior transplantation of Hedgehog-expressing cells induced mirror-image limb duplications.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E and described in the Results section.

claim: Bmp and Wnt signals establish dorsoventral polarity in vertebrate and arthropod limbs.
source: Bmp and Wnt signals, which establish dorsoventral polarity in vertebrate and arthropod limbs, are similarly polarized in cuttlefish.
evidence: This is based on cited literature about vertebrate and arthropod limb development.

claim: Bmp and Wnt signals are similarly polarized in cuttlefish limbs as in vertebrate and arthropod limbs.
source: Bmp and Wnt signals, which establish dorsoventral polarity in vertebrate and arthropod limbs, are similarly polarized in cuttlefish.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Inhibition of Bmp2/4 dorsally caused ectopic expression of Notum in cuttlefish limbs.
source: Inhibition of Bmp2/4 dorsally caused ectopic expression of Notum, which marks the ventral sucker field, and ectopic sucker development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Noggin bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Notum marks the ventral sucker field in cuttlefish limbs.
source: Inhibition of Bmp2/4 dorsally caused ectopic expression of Notum, which marks the ventral sucker field, and ectopic sucker development.
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3N-Q.

claim: Inhibition of Bmp2/4 dorsally caused ectopic sucker development in cuttlefish limbs.
source: Inhibition of Bmp2/4 dorsally caused ectopic expression of Notum, which marks the ventral sucker field, and ectopic sucker development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Noggin bead experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cuttlefish show proximodistal regionalization of Hth, Exd, Dll, Dac, Sp8/9, and Wnt expression.
source: Cuttlefish also show proximodistal regionalization of Hth, Exd, Dll, Dac, Sp8/9, and Wnt expression, which delineates arm and tentacle sucker fields.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Proximodistal regionalization of gene expression delineates arm and tentacle sucker fields in cuttlefish.
source: Cuttlefish also show proximodistal regionalization of Hth, Exd, Dll, Dac, Sp8/9, and Wnt expression, which delineates arm and tentacle sucker fields.
evidence: This is supported by comparing gene expression patterns with morphological boundaries shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: Cephalopod limbs evolved by parallel activation of a genetic program for appendage development that was present in the bilaterian common ancestor.
source: These results suggest that cephalopod limbs evolved by parallel activation of a genetic program for appendage development that was present in the bilaterian common ancestor.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the conservation of developmental mechanisms across cephalopods, arthropods, and vertebrates.

claim: Animal appendages have widely varying morphologies and perform a multitude of functions, including locomotion, feeding, and reproduction.
source: Animal appendages have widely varying morphologies and perform a multitude of functions, including locomotion, feeding, and reproduction (Nielsen, 2012; Ruppert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Limbs evolved on multiple occasions in animals.
source: Limbs evolved on multiple occasions, and the absence of shared ontogenetic or morphological precursors of appendages in many animal lineages is consistent with their independent origins (Minelli, 2003; Pueyo and Couso, 2005; Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology supported by citations.

claim: The absence of shared ontogenetic or morphological precursors of appendages in many animal lineages is consistent with their independent origins.
source: Limbs evolved on multiple occasions, and the absence of shared ontogenetic or morphological precursors of appendages in many animal lineages is consistent with their independent origins (Minelli, 2003; Pueyo and Couso, 2005; Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological and developmental studies cited in the literature.

claim: Appendages in different clades of Bilateria are non-homologous morphological innovations that arose by convergent evolution.
source: This has led to the view that appendages in different clades of Bilateria are non-homologous morphological innovations that arose by convergent evolution (Nielsen, 2012; Ruppert et al., 2004).
evidence: This represents a historical view in the field supported by citations.

claim: The independently evolved limbs of arthropods and vertebrates share developmental genetic similarities despite more than 500 million years of divergence.
source: However, despite more than 500 million years of divergence, the independently evolved limbs of arthropods and vertebrates share developmental genetic similarities (Pueyo and Couso, 2005; Shubin et al., 1997; Tabin et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous comparative developmental studies.

claim: Little is known about molecular mechanisms of limb development in Spiralia.
source: A major obstacle to resolving this question is that the evidence of a conserved program derives almost exclusively from Ecdysozoa and Deuterostomia (Pueyo and Couso, 2005; Shubin et al., 1997), and little is known about molecular mechanisms of limb development in Spiralia, the third major superphylum of Bilateria (Grimmel et al., 2016; Prpic, 2008; Winchell and Jacobs, 2013; Winchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on a review of the existing literature on spiralian development.

claim: Mollusca is the largest lineage within spiralians.
source: Within spiralians, the phylum Mollusca is the largest lineage, displaying a rich diversity of body plans (Figure 1A) dating back to the Cambrian explosion (Ruppert et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established taxonomic and phylogenetic knowledge.

claim: Mollusca displays a rich diversity of body plans dating back to the Cambrian explosion.
source: Within spiralians, the phylum Mollusca is the largest lineage, displaying a rich diversity of body plans (Figure 1A) dating back to the Cambrian explosion (Ruppert et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1A and cited literature.

claim: The evolution of arms and tentacles in cephalopod mollusks contributed to the successful adaptive radiation of these agile marine predators.
source: The evolution of arms and tentacles in cephalopod mollusks contributed to the successful adaptive radiation of these agile marine predators (Kröger et al., 2011; Ruppert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of cephalopod evolutionary history supported by citations.

claim: Cephalopod limbs are highly muscular appendages that bear cup-shaped suckers on their ventral sides.
source: Cephalopod limbs are highly muscular appendages that bear cup-shaped suckers on their ventral sides.
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by images in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Arms are short and have suckers along the entire ventral surface.
source: Arms are short and have suckers along the entire ventral surface (Figure 1B and C), whereas tentacles are longer, retractable appendages with suckers restricted to a distal pad (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Tentacles are longer, retractable appendages with suckers restricted to a distal pad.
source: Arms are short and have suckers along the entire ventral surface (Figure 1B and C), whereas tentacles are longer, retractable appendages with suckers restricted to a distal pad (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Tentacles are thought to be specialized serial homologs of the arms.
source: Tentacles are thought to be specialized serial homologs of the arms (Arnold, 1965; Lemaire, 1970; Shigeno et al., 2008) and are present in decapods (squid and cuttlefish) but absent in nautilids and octopods.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Tentacles are present in decapods (squid and cuttlefish) but absent in nautilids and octopods.
source: Tentacles are thought to be specialized serial homologs of the arms (Arnold, 1965; Lemaire, 1970; Shigeno et al., 2008) and are present in decapods (squid and cuttlefish) but absent in nautilids and octopods.
evidence: This is established taxonomic knowledge about cephalopod morphology.

claim: Limbs likely evolved de novo in cephalopods.
source: Limbs likely evolved de novo in cephalopods (Figure 1A), since no homologous precursor structures have been identified in any other mollusk lineages (Lee et al., 2003; Shigeno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from comparative morphology and phylogenetic analysis supported by citations.

claim: No homologous precursor structures to cephalopod limbs have been identified in any other mollusk lineages.
source: Limbs likely evolved de novo in cephalopods (Figure 1A), since no homologous precursor structures have been identified in any other mollusk lineages (Lee et al., 2003; Shigeno et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological studies cited in the literature.

claim: Cuttlefishes have five bilaterally symmetric limb pairs (ten limbs; eight arms and two tentacles).
source: Cuttlefishes have five bilaterally symmetric limb pairs (ten limbs; eighth arms and two tentacles).
evidence: This is a morphological description supported by images in Figure 1.

claim: The first sign of limb formation in cuttlefish is observed at stage 16 as small swellings around the periphery of a flat-shaped embryo.
source: The first sign of limb formation is observed at stage 16, when all ten limb primordia (five on each side) can be detected as small swellings around the periphery of a flat-shaped embryo, which lies at the top of the large yolk mass (Figure 1H and M).
evidence: This is based on developmental observations shown in Figure 1H and M.

claim: Initiation of limb outgrowth in cuttlefish is caused by localized cell proliferation.
source: Analysis of the mitotic marker phospho-histone H3 (PHH3) at stage 15 revealed localized clusters of PHH3-positive cells in each of the early limb primordia (Figure 1F and G), indicating that initiation of limb outgrowth is caused by localized cell proliferation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PHH3 immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Discrete limb buds are observed from stage 17 in cuttlefish.
source: Discrete limb buds are observed from stage 17 (Figure 1I and N; Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is based on developmental observations shown in Figure 1I and N.

claim: A sucker field primordium initially forms as a narrow proximodistal ridge along the ventral surface of each cuttlefish limb.
source: Analysis of sucker development showed that a sucker field primordium initially forms as a narrow proximodistal ridge along the ventral surface of each limb (evident by stage 21; Figure 1P).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations shown in Figure 1P.

claim: The sucker field ridge cleaves superficially, segregating sucker buds from proximal to distal.
source: At later stages, the sucker field ridge cleaves superficially, segregating sucker buds from proximal to distal (Figure 1Q).
evidence: This is based on SEM observations shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: Sucker buds form in four parallel rows across the anteroposterior axis in cuttlefish arms.
source: As the arms elongate, the sucker buds are laid down on the entire ventral surface of each arm (Figure 1L and R; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C–G), forming four parallel rows across the anteroposterior axis (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sucker buds form in eight rows along the anteroposterior axis of the tentacle sucker pads.
source: In the tentacles, the primordial sucker band is restricted to the distal tip, where sucker buds form in eight rows along the anteroposterior axis of the tentacle sucker pads (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The full complement of immature sucker bud rows is present on each limb at hatching in cuttlefish.
source: The full complement of immature sucker bud rows is present on each limb at hatching, and differentiation of the suckers continues during post-hatch development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This is based on developmental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: Differentiation of the suckers continues during post-hatch development in cuttlefish.
source: The full complement of immature sucker bud rows is present on each limb at hatching, and differentiation of the suckers continues during post-hatch development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This is based on developmental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: Exd and Hth are restricted proximally in cuttlefish limb buds.
source: Genes that pattern the proximodistal axis of arthropod and vertebrate limbs (Lecuit and Cohen, 1997; Mercader et al., 1999; Panganiban et al., 1997; Pueyo and Couso, 2005) showed similarly polarized patterns of expression along the proximodistal axis of cuttlefish limb buds, with Exd and Hth restricted proximally (Figure 2B,F and G; Figure 3A–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,I and J)
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Dll, Dac, Sp8/9a, Wnt1, Wnt5, and Wnt7 are restricted distally in cuttlefish limb buds.
source: and Dll, Dac, Sp8/9a, Wnt1, Wnt5, and Wnt7 restricted distally (Figure 2C,H–J; Figure 3F–I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E and L–N; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C,G,I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The distal expression boundaries of Exd and Hth and the proximal expression boundaries of Dll and Sp8/9a mark the morphological boundary between the proximal sucker-free and the distal sucker-forming regions in cuttlefish limbs.
source: At stages 20–21, the distal expression boundaries of Exd and Hth and the proximal expression boundaries of Dll and Sp8/9a appear to mark the morphological boundary between the proximal sucker-free and the distal sucker-forming regions (compare right panels in Figure 2F–H and J with Figure 1P).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing gene expression patterns with morphological boundaries.

claim: The Exd/Hth expression domains extend further distally in tentacles compared to arms.
source: Indeed, at stages when arms and tentacles begin to develop their distinctive morphologies -- tentacles are longer and have an extensive proximal sucker-free domain -- the Exd/Hth expression domains were found to extend further distally in tentacles (Figure 3B,D) compared to arms (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing gene expression patterns between arms and tentacles shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The distal expansion of the Exd/Hth expression domain matches the expanded sucker-free region and the distal restriction of suckers in tentacles.
source: This distal expansion of the Exd/Hth expression domain matches the expanded sucker-free region and the distal restriction of suckers in tentacles (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a correlation between gene expression and morphology shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hh expression is restricted to the anterior margin of cuttlefish limb buds.
source: We analyzed Hh expression during cuttlefish limb development at stages 16 to 20 and found that Hh expression is also polarized to one side of cuttlefish limb buds. In cuttlefishes, however, Hh expression is restricted to the anterior margin of the limb bud, whereas in arthropods and vertebrates, Hh/Shh is expressed posteriorly (Figure 2D and K; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D, K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In arthropods and vertebrates, Hh/Shh is expressed posteriorly in limb buds.
source: In cuttlefishes, however, Hh expression is restricted to the anterior margin of the limb bud, whereas in arthropods and vertebrates, Hh/Shh is expressed posteriorly (Figure 2D and K; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature about arthropod and vertebrate limb development.

claim: Patched is expressed in an anterior-to-posterior gradient in cuttlefish limb buds.
source: Consistent with the anterior localization of Hh, we detected expression of Patched, which serves as a readout of Hedgehog signal transduction, in an anterior-to-posterior gradient (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Anteroposteriorly restricted activation of the Hedgehog pathway is a conserved feature of cephalopod, arthropod, and vertebrate limb development.
source: Thus, anteroposteriorly restricted activation of the Hedgehog pathway is a conserved feature of cephalopod, arthropod, and vertebrate limb development, but the polarity of the signaling center is reversed in cephalopod limbs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing Hh expression patterns across these lineages.

claim: The polarity of the Hedgehog signaling center is reversed in cephalopod limbs compared to arthropod and vertebrate limbs.
source: Thus, anteroposteriorly restricted activation of the Hedgehog pathway is a conserved feature of cephalopod, arthropod, and vertebrate limb development, but the polarity of the signaling center is reversed in cephalopod limbs.
evidence: This is based on comparing Hh expression patterns shown in the data.

claim: By stage 21, the anteriorly restricted Hh domain has diminished and a new, central expression domain appears in the location of the brachial nerve primordia.
source: By stage 21, the anteriorly restricted Hh domain has diminished and a new, central expression domain appears in the location of the brachial nerve primordia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,K.

claim: The dorsoventral axis is controlled by the antagonistic actions of wg/Wnt and dpp/Bmp signaling in arthropods and vertebrates.
source: We then examined the dorsoventral axis, which is controlled by the antagonistic actions of wg/Wnt and dpp/Bmp signaling in arthropods and vertebrates (Brook and Cohen, 1996; Cygan et al., 1997; Diaz-Benjumea et al., 1994; Jiang and Struhl, 1996; Parr and McMahon, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: In arthropods, the Wnt ligand wg is expressed ventrally.
source: In arthropods, the Wnt ligand wg is expressed ventrally, whereas the Bmp2/4 ortholog dpp is expressed dorsally (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Diaz-Benjumea et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: In arthropods, the Bmp2/4 ortholog dpp is expressed dorsally.
source: In arthropods, the Wnt ligand wg is expressed ventrally, whereas the Bmp2/4 ortholog dpp is expressed dorsally (Basler and Struhl, 1994; Diaz-Benjumea et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Expression and function of the Wnt-Bmp network is conserved, albeit with inverted polarity, in vertebrate limbs.
source: Expression and function of the Wnt-Bmp network is conserved, albeit with inverted polarity, in vertebrate limbs; Wnt7a is expressed dorsally (Parr and McMahon, 1995) and Bmp signaling activates Engrailed1 (En1) ventrally (Ahn et al., 2001), and these interactions regulate development of dorsal and ventral limb structures (Cygan et al., 1997; Parr and McMahon, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Wnt7a is expressed dorsally in vertebrate limbs.
source: Expression and function of the Wnt-Bmp network is conserved, albeit with inverted polarity, in vertebrate limbs; Wnt7a is expressed dorsally (Parr and McMahon, 1995) and Bmp signaling activates Engrailed1 (En1) ventrally (Ahn et al., 2001), and these interactions regulate development of dorsal and ventral limb structures (Cygan et al., 1997; Parr and McMahon, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Bmp signaling activates Engrailed1 (En1) ventrally in vertebrate limbs.
source: Expression and function of the Wnt-Bmp network is conserved, albeit with inverted polarity, in vertebrate limbs; Wnt7a is expressed dorsally (Parr and McMahon, 1995) and Bmp signaling activates Engrailed1 (En1) ventrally (Ahn et al., 2001), and these interactions regulate development of dorsal and ventral limb structures (Cygan et al., 1997; Parr and McMahon, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Bmp2/4 and En show dorsally polarized expression during cuttlefish limb development.
source: During cuttlefish limb development, Bmp2/4 and En show dorsally polarized expression (Figure 2E,M and N; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2E, M, N and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Genes encoding Wnt ligands (Wnt1, Wnt5 and Wnt7) and cellular components of canonical Wnt signaling cascade (Tcf3/4 and Frz9/10) are expressed broadly throughout the dorsoventral axis of cuttlefish limb buds.
source: Genes encoding Wnt ligands (Wnt1, Wnt5 and Wnt7) and cellular components of canonical Wnt signaling cascade (Tcf3/4 and Frz9/10) are expressed broadly throughout the dorsoventral axis of cuttlefish limb buds (Figure 3F–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1L–R; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G,I and J)
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The secreted Wnt antagonists Notum and Sfrp1/2/5 are expressed dorsally in the limb and interlimb regions of cuttlefish.
source: however, the secreted Wnt antagonists Notum and Sfrp1/2/5 are expressed dorsally in the limb and interlimb regions (Figure 3J–M), with the Sfrp1/2/5 domain extending deeper into the dorsal limb buds (Figure 2O; Figure 3M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2O, Figure 3J-M.

claim: The Sfrp1/2/5 domain extends deeper into the dorsal limb buds than Notum in cuttlefish.
source: however, the secreted Wnt antagonists Notum and Sfrp1/2/5 are expressed dorsally in the limb and interlimb regions (Figure 3J–M), with the Sfrp1/2/5 domain extending deeper into the dorsal limb buds (Figure 2O; Figure 3M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing expression patterns in Figure 2O and Figure 3M.

claim: Dorsal expression of Wnt antagonists suggests a mechanism for restriction of Wnt signaling to the ventral side of the cephalopod limb buds.
source: This dorsal expression of Wnt antagonists suggests a mechanism for restriction of Wnt signaling to the ventral side of the cephalopod limb buds.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression patterns of Wnt antagonists.

claim: The genetic pathways active along the proximodistal, anteroposterior, and dorsoventral axes of cephalopod limbs are homologous (specifically, orthologous) to the networks that regulate limb development in arthropods and vertebrates.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the genetic pathways active along the proximodistal, anteroposterior, and dorsoventral axes of cephalopod limbs are homologous (specifically, orthologous) to the networks that regulate limb development in arthropods and vertebrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of gene expression patterns and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Implantation of Noggin beads on the dorsal side of cuttlefish limb buds resulted in ectopic, dorsal expansion of the Notum mRNA domain.
source: Implantation of Nog beads on the dorsal side of cuttlefish limb buds resulted in ectopic, dorsal expansion of the Notum mRNA domain (n = 3/3; control PBS [phosphate buffered saline] beads had no effect on Notum expression [n = 3/3]) (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Control PBS beads had no effect on Notum expression in cuttlefish limb buds.
source: Implantation of Nog beads on the dorsal side of cuttlefish limb buds resulted in ectopic, dorsal expansion of the Notum mRNA domain (n = 3/3; control PBS [phosphate buffered saline] beads had no effect on Notum expression [n = 3/3]) (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Noggin-treated limbs developed ectopic sucker buds on the dorsal surface.
source: Analysis of limb morphology by scanning electron microscopy revealed the presence of ectopic sucker buds on the dorsal surface of Nog-treated limbs (n = 8/12; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: In limbs that received control PBS beads dorsally, sucker buds were restricted to ventral surface.
source: By contrast, in limbs that received control PBS beads dorsally, sucker buds were restricted to ventral surface and terminated at the normal dorsal-ventral boundary at the tip of the limb (n = 15/15; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dorsal Bmp2/4 activity is required for the early specification of dorsal identity in cephalopod limb development.
source: Our finding that antagonism of Bmp signaling results in development of ventral structures (sucker buds) on the dorsal side of the limb indicates that dorsal Bmp2/4 activity is required for the early specification of dorsal identity in cephalopod limb development.
evidence: This is inferred from the Noggin bead experiments showing ectopic ventral structures after Bmp inhibition.

claim: Transplantation of Hh-expressing cells to the posterior side of cuttlefish limb buds resulted in posterior limb duplications.
source: Transplantation of Hh-expressing cells to the posterior side of cuttlefish limb buds resulted in posterior limb duplications (n = 7/12; Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The posterior duplications induced by Hh-expressing cell grafts contained sucker buds.
source: Analysis of morphology and gene expression in host limbs approximately 10 days after receiving the graft revealed that the posterior duplications even contained sucker buds, which were marked by Notum expression (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4I-J.

claim: Limbs that received control grafts of stage 24 funnel epithelium that lacks Hh expression developed normally.
source: By contrast, limbs that received control grafts of stage 24 funnel epithelium that lacks Hh expression (Tarazona et al., 2016) developed normally (n = 8/8; Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Transitory treatment of cuttlefish embryos at stage 16 with cyclopamine disrupted the anteroposterior distribution of sucker rows in arms and tentacles.
source: Transitory treatment (2 days) of cuttlefish embryos at stage 16, when Hh is first expressed on the anterior side of the early limb bud, with the small molecule cyclopamine, an inhibitor of Smoothened that represses Hh signaling (Figure 4K), disrupted the anteroposterior distribution of sucker rows in arms and tentacles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4K-O.

claim: Cyclopamine is an inhibitor of Smoothened that represses Hh signaling.
source: Transitory treatment (2 days) of cuttlefish embryos at stage 16, when Hh is first expressed on the anterior side of the early limb bud, with the small molecule cyclopamine, an inhibitor of Smoothened that represses Hh signaling (Figure 4K), disrupted the anteroposterior distribution of sucker rows in arms and tentacles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of cyclopamine.

claim: Cyclopamine-treated embryos showed arms with a reduced number of suckers and sucker rows.
source: Severity of this phenotype ranged from arms with a reduced number of suckers and sucker rows (n = 10/10; Figure 4N and O) to completely sucker-free tentacles (n = 8/10; Figure 4L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4N-O.

claim: Cyclopamine-treated embryos showed completely sucker-free tentacles.
source: Severity of this phenotype ranged from arms with a reduced number of suckers and sucker rows (n = 10/10; Figure 4N and O) to completely sucker-free tentacles (n = 8/10; Figure 4L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Control treatments with vehicle only (DMSO) did not alter the normal anteroposterior pattern of sucker rows.
source: Control treatments with vehicle only (DMSO) did not alter the normal anteroposterior pattern of sucker rows (n = 8/8; Figure 4M and P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 4M and P.

claim: The brachial nerve cords develop in both cyclopamine and DMSO treated embryos.
source: Finally, to confirm that the phenotype of cyclopamine-treated embryos was not due to failure in brachial nerve differentiation, we examined acetylated tubulin immunofluorescence, which shows that the brachial nerve cords develop in both cyclopamine and DMSO treated embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Hh signaling is necessary for proper patterning of the anteroposterior axis in cephalopod limb development.
source: These results show that Hh signaling is necessary for proper patterning of the anteroposterior axis in cephalopod limb development.
evidence: This is inferred from the cyclopamine experiments showing disrupted anteroposterior patterning.

claim: The proximodistal, dorsoventral, and anteroposterior axes of cuttlefish limb buds are patterned by the same pathways that regulate arthropod and vertebrate limb development.
source: Our finding that the proximodistal, dorsoventral, and anteroposterior axes of cuttlefish limb buds are patterned by the same pathways that regulate arthropod and vertebrate limb development suggests that the independent evolution of limbs in cephalopod mollusks involved recruitment of an ancient genetic program for appendage development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the gene expression and functional data presented.

claim: The independent evolution of limbs in cephalopod mollusks involved recruitment of an ancient genetic program for appendage development.
source: Our finding that the proximodistal, dorsoventral, and anteroposterior axes of cuttlefish limb buds are patterned by the same pathways that regulate arthropod and vertebrate limb development suggests that the independent evolution of limbs in cephalopod mollusks involved recruitment of an ancient genetic program for appendage development.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of developmental mechanisms across independently evolved limbs.

claim: Discovery of this appendage developmental circuit within Spiralia demonstrates its deep conservation across all three branches of Bilateria (i.e., Deuterostomia, Ecdysozoa, and Spiralia).
source: Discovery of this appendage developmental circuit within Spiralia demonstrates its deep conservation across all three branches of Bilateria (i.e., Deuterostomia, Ecdysozoa, and Spiralia), suggesting its presence in the common ancestor of all bilaterians (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the developmental program across all three bilaterian superphyla.

claim: The appendage developmental circuit was present in the common ancestor of all bilaterians.

evidence: This is inferred from the deep conservation across all three bilaterian superphyla.

claim: The diversity in the number of sucker rows in cephalopod limbs could be explained by modulation of Hh signaling.
source: Likewise, the results of functional manipulations of Hh signaling in cuttlefish limbs suggests that the diversity in the number of sucker rows in cephalopod limbs (i.e. four rows in squids and cuttlefishes, two in octopus, and one in vampire squid and glass octopus) could be explained by modulation of Hh signaling, in the same way that gradual changes to Shh regulation has led to variation in digit number in tetrapod vertebrates (Scherz et al., 2007; Shapiro et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2008).

claim: Homologous developmental mechanisms underlie the multiple parallel origins of limbs in bilaterians.
source: Finally, we note that while the data presented here point to the existence of a deeply conserved genetic program for appendage development across Bilateria, this does not imply that the limbs of cephalopods, arthropods, and vertebrates are homologous structures, or that limbs were present in the common ancestor. Rather, these results show that homologous developmental mechanisms underlie the multiple parallel origins of limbs in bilaterians.
evidence: This is the main conclusion about the relationship between developmental mechanism conservation and morphological homology.
